Venezuela Extends Quarantine Measures as Respiratory Virus Outbreak Hampers Economic Activity

CARACAS, June 17—Venezuelan authorities have extended a nationwide quarantine for a third consecutive week as a severe outbreak of the so-called “Caracas Respiratory Virus” (CRV-24) spreads rapidly, disrupting daily life and deepening economic challenges across the country.

President Lorena Silva, in a televised address Monday, announced that all schools, non-essential businesses, and public gatherings would remain shuttered until at least June 28. Public transportation is operating at reduced capacity, with checkpoints in place on major highways to enforce movement restrictions.

“We are acting to protect public health and save lives,” Silva said. “The virus is not yet under control, and premature reopening would be irresponsible.”

The Ministry of Health reported 3,412 new CRV-24 cases in the past 24 hours, bringing the total to 41,800 confirmed infections and 1,125 deaths since the outbreak began in early May. Hospitals in Caracas and Maracaibo are reportedly nearing capacity, with temporary field clinics established in several states.

The quarantine has sharply curtailed economic activity in the already fragile nation. The Venezuelan Chamber of Retailers estimates daily sales have dropped by 70% since the restrictions began. “Many small businesses lack the reserves to survive prolonged closures,” said Luis Páez, the chamber’s president. “We urge the government to consider targeted relief for affected sectors.”

Food distribution has also been disrupted, leading to long queues at supermarkets and sporadic shortages of staples such as rice and cooking oil. Truck drivers’ union leader Maritza González reported that roadblocks and curfews have delayed deliveries. “We need clear protocols to ensure essential goods reach every region,” González said.

Despite growing frustration, public health officials warn against easing measures prematurely. “CRV-24 spreads quickly and can overwhelm our health system,” said Dr. Helena Armas, head of infectious diseases at Central University Hospital. “Strict distancing remains our best defense.”

Authorities have pledged to review the restrictions weekly, but officials say reopening will depend on a sustained decline in new infections.
